Should Schools Provide Free Pads and Tampons?
Have you ever experienced period shaming, or 'period poverty'?
Should schools step in to help?

How are pads and tampons similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools?
How are they different?
In my opinion, I think they should be provided as needed.
It's a reality that girls go through 'that time of the month.' Hygiene products are a basic need.
It's a fact of life.
Some families provide them for adolescents.
Some families don't for a variety of reasons.
Sometimes families are too poor and can't afford to buy feminine hygiene products.
Some families are neglectful and simply don't make it a priority to provide these products.
It would be a shame for a student to be in school and not have a pad or tampon when it is needed.
So, it's up to schools to be prepared.
Every school should have a plan.
Just like they have a plan if a student falls and needs ice for her knee, or a band-aid or if there's an emergency, there should be a plan if someone needs a feminine hygiene product.

No one wants to go back to the nurse and say, 'I need a pad.' There should be a designated place in every restroom.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, all the screen time for online schools, online work from home or remote work it going to have a very bad impact on us socially.
Sooner or later people will become anti-social.
People will forget how to deal with others in person.
People will lose their patience.
We will develop problems communicating with others due to the mostly the loss of personal connection with others.
We have seen this in the development of gaming for instance.

What seems like a long time ago, if you wanted to play a multiplayer game, you had multiple controllers, food, snacks, drinks, and your friends would come over to your house to play (or you would go to theirs).
These friends were not complete strangers.
Sure, there was fun loving jibbing each other sometimes, but no one felt like they were really under personal attack.
Today if you play a game online, you stay at home and connect your PC or console to the internet and join an online game.
Gamers have become toxic to each other across because there is no longer a sense of personal connectedness or friendship at all.
It's easy to call someone a loser when there is no consequences for said action.
The same thing will take place across screens for work and school as time goes by.
People will not feel that sense of comradery at work anymore.
Kids won't develop a social sense of friendship with kids outside the home anymore, and teachers won't feel as dedicated to their students or bosses to their employees.
Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news?
Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world?
Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all?
Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, keeping up with the news is very important.
I think everyone should have some background knowledge about what's going on in the world, even if they don't follow it closely.
It helps to shape your world view and helps you form your own opinions.
This pandemic is a perfect example of what happens when certain people do not follow the news.
Those who don't follow the news are often in denial of realities like this.
People have denied that coronavirus exists despite the news telling them otherwise.
Some people even seem proud to ignore news unless it is conspiracy theory based.
That's why many Republicans believe that Donald Trump won the 2020 election.
They only listen to news that is extreme and doesn't report the actual truth or they don't listen to the news at all and just listen to their friends.
These people are proud to be American but they are not doing their duty to be informed.
I think it's too vague to just say people keep up with the news or not.
Even if you do watch the news, you may not be watching a very informative program.
Morning shows for example tend to be more sugar coated.
People watch it to stay informed but aren't getting as much information.
Often times you need to watch national news to hear what is really going on in our country.
Sometimes people want to avoid such grim news so they prefer the friendly morning show format.
However they need to know what is happening.
If people do not know what's happening in their own country, they cannot hold their leaders accountable.
That's exactly why Donald Trump did not lose by a landslide.
People weren't informed.
That's all there is to it.
So yes, I do think people have some responsibility to know what is going on.
Otherwise they can't make informed decisions and when things go wrong they are partially to blame.
They may try to shift the blame but they are just as at fault as the next uninformed American.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, there are advantages of listening to an audiobook.
It does allow you to enjoy a book while you are doing other things.
It allows you to enjoy a book without getting a headache from reading.
You can use the time to sit in the bathtub and just listen.
That can be very relaxing.
It also allows you more time to hear the story especially when driving.
Imagine going on a cross country trip and bringing audiobooks with you.
You could easily get through multiple books even while driving.
If you had brought regular books then you might have been lucky to get through one in your downtime.
There are disadvantages to listening to an audiobook.
You don't get that connection that you otherwise would have had from holding the physical book.
Also out of sight out of mind comes into play as well.
If you don't see a physical book sitting on your coffee table then it can be easy to forget that you were even reading in the first place.
That's part of living a hectic life.
It's gotten so easy to access audiobooks that they are just as available as physical books now.
You can even download them for free via your library's app.
No longer do you need to pay for an audiobook.
That is a game changer.
So which is the right choice, an audio book or a regular book?
I think that depends on what your situation is and why you are reading.
If you are busy and and otherwise wouldn't have time to read then an audiobook is a great choice.
If you however have more free time then you can't beat a regular book.
The most important thing though is to just keep taking in these stories that are available to us.
The way they are delivered isn't as important as just doing it.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, a person is ultimately the one that dictates the level of risk and or safety they can undertake in their life.
What they decide to do with their life, is primarily their decision.
Risky sports such as extreme mountain climbing, is an active decision that people take, just like other athletes that perform less risky sports.
Extreme sports are not for everyone, but for those that do choose to participate, it is their choice to do so.
They are not forced to do so, nor are the dangers hidden from them when they being investing time in the sport.

Less dangerous sports will always draw more people to it, primarily for the ease in getting proficient in said sports, but also the fact that such sports will not injure them if precautions are taken.
The same can be applied to extreme sports, as mountain climbing can be done in a risky manner, or in a way that minimizes dangers and reduces the risk for the person.

Whether a sport is then too dangerous does not change its classification, as sports are labeled not based on the risk involved in the sport, but rather how the person engages in it, and whether they compete or even cooperate with others.
Extreme sports follow the same set of guidelines as many less risky sports, but are associated with more risk.
For example, people wishing to mountain climb must learn proper techniques, invest in proper equipment, and even train on less tasking mountains before tackling more dangerous and demanding climbs.
The same is true for other extreme sports.
As for when a sport becomes unreasonable or still within reason depends primarily on the person, specifically their skill, physique, and mindset.
For example, a person who is not in good physical shape, or does not have the proper mindset to climb a mountain, will be more likely to get injured on the climb than a more experienced climber.
Thus we could say for the person that it is unreasonable for them to continue to mountain climb, until they get more experience and training.

There might as well be some level that is unobtainable for athletes and participants of an extreme sport, that might be considered based on risk and danger to be unreasonable to undertake no matter the physique and training said participants may have.
Ideally, they ought to be well informed of the risks and dangers, and well-prepared for the sport.
To disregard such considerations is to make the sport more risky than it already is, but many do make such considerations.

n the end, it is up to the person to decide what they are willing to risk in their life., and what sort of achievements they wish to accomplish, either for the notoriety or for some sense of self-worth.

Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, college athletes should definitely get paid and thinking otherwise is ridiculous.
Very simply put, the athletes make the universities an insane amount of money and never see a dollar of it.
The argument that they are getting a scholarship which is a payment is a ridiculous one to me.
Sure they are getting a scholarship.
They also are working much harder than the typical student.
Student athletes are basically being a full time student and a full time athlete at the same time.
Thankfully, a bill was just passed that allows students to make money off of their name and their likeness.
I would be willing to bet than an athlete like Zion Williamson made Duke at least 20 times the amount that his scholarship was.
The student athletes have simply been exploited by colleges in the past, and the only people who see no issues with that are the universities themselves.
The entire student athletes getting a scholarship thing is a scam.
It's just a scam that the universities and the top 1%  push because it helps make them money.
Paying student athletes would not destroy college sports.
Would it have an effect on the sports economy?
Sure.
Instead of the universities and networks keeping 100% of the profits and getting rich off of the student athletes, they'll have to give them their fair share.
Anyone who disagrees with students not getting paid for sports simply wants to exploit them.
There is no reason why a student should be risking injury before they go pro for a university for free.
I don't want to hear the scholarship excuse.
Students could have a full ride for academics.
Then what happens to those students?
They get a full ride for academics and them playing sports gets them nothing extra?
Maybe a free textbook or free lunches from the school cafeteria?
We have finally figured out that this scam has been going on for too long and that is why the lawmakers made a change.
The exploitation of these 18-22 year old men and women is disgusting.
I'm extremely happy that it is changing.
There have been so many student athletes in the past that have been used by their university.
If people ever saw the amount of money that Alabama makes from their football program, their jaws would drop.
That goes the same for Duke and North Carolina for basketball.
That goes for basically all of the SEC and ACC teams in college football.
There is enough money being made off of the college athletes to spread the wealth.
I do think there should be a cap on it and/or there should be a GPA to maintain in order to get their payments.
If they fall below a 2.0 GPA for example they get fined or something along those lines to teach them the consequences of slacking off.
Most college athletes won't go pro so they still need to make sure their academics are a priority.
As long as their grades are in good standing, they should get their payments.
We have had enough of students being exploited by the people in power.
That exploitation is now dead and students will get the money that they rightfully deserve.

In my opinion, stereotypical characters have no place in any story.
They betray a deadening lack of imagination and creativity on the part of their creators.
A stereotyped character is a kind of lazy short-cut, used by a writer who has no real faith in their own work.
I don't like those types of creators, so I typically avoid their work, whether it is in books, games, movies, or television.
So, my experience with these kinds of characters is limited.
However, some of the characters I've encountered that made me cringe that readily spring to mind include Harry Potter, Rey from the recent Star Wars films, and Abby from The Last of Us 2.

Harry Potter 's portrayal as a wide-eyed twit who has to be saved by everyone else, succeeds without without any particular effort on his part but instead through his status as a 'chosen one'  was particularly eye-roll inducing; I always rooted against him, and I've avoided every Harry Potter movie since the first.
Star Wars: The Force Awakens ' Rey is a straight up Mary Sue, with no particular flaws or accomplishments.
She proceeds through the stories in a similar way to Harry Potter, and these are basically male and female versions of the exact same type of stereotypical 'chosen one' character.
As a result of Rey, I gave up on the new Star Wars movies entirely.

Abby from The Last of Us was an unmitigated stereotype of an ugly, muscle-bound, violent, 'trans' or lesbian character that was included specifically to appeal to some potentially less-savory segments of the gaming audience, and I found her unbelievably offensive, and stopped playing the game within 15 minutes of having to endure her.
There are many older stereotypes in all media, of course.

But I guess the point I'm trying to make, is that there isn't any special quality about stereotypes, they're just examples of poor writing, laziness and creative bankruptcy, and the stories that feature them are bad, and not worth watching.
The burden is on the consumer, to avoid bad work, and support good work, and that includes work featuring offensive stereotypes, as well as any other kind of objectionable features.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news?
Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world?
Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all?
Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, good citizens should be expected to keep reasonably informed about the news, both national and international.
The ancient Greeks, who we model much of our own civilization from, judged a man a fool who did not understand the affairs of the day.
I think that is a good standard to hold ourselves to.
Some might feel that they should just be left alone to mange their own business, without needing to know what is going on in the world around them.
However, nobody in modern society is an island.
A well-informed population is especially important in democratic systems.
If people are not informed, they cannot make informed decisions about who to vote for, or what laws to support.
The morality and justness of a democracy hinges on the population making reasonable and informed decisions.
In this light we can see that it is selfish and dangerous to allow ourselves to be ignorant of the news.
Society only works when people are responsible not only for themselves but for each other and for the community as a whole.
We can only act to help our community when we are educated about the issues it faces.
For these reasons we must all take the responsibility to learn the news and to understand it.
In this way we can move together wisely into a better world.

But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'

The concussion syndrome linked to contact sports like football is a prime example.
College athletics has become a huge money machine.
Big sports program schools have been willing and have paid top dollar for a few select athletes so that is not going to change.
College athletes should be given the opportunity to receive compensation as well.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?
Would you be surprised to hear that a study found that research subjects were more upset by stories of a dog beaten by a baseball bat than of an adult similarly beaten?
Or that other researchers found that if forced to choose, 40 percent of people would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist.
Why do you think many people are more empathetic toward the suffering of animals than that of people?
In your opinion, is it wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering?
Why do you think so?
In my opinion, people are more empathetic to animals because we tend to regard animals as innocent and defenseless.
Humans are capable of reasoning and rationalizing, as well as making decisions.
They understand the things that are causing their suffering, and they are capable of changing their lives, actions, or environments in order to alleviate it.
Animals, on the other hand, cannot mediate their suffering in this way.

A suffering human can often escape the forces causing their pain, while a suffering animal stays in its environment and is incapable of finding relief, unless chance or death, or a concerned human, intervenes to bring them relief.
We also tend to view humans as responsible for their own suffering, while animals are seen as non-volitional, innocent, and deserving of sympathy.
In other words, a suffering human is often viewed as 'getting what they deserve', while a miserable animal is seen as pitiful and undeserving of their suffering.
To a certain extent, these things are true.
Humans are different than animals, and have much greater capacity to reason and make decisions, and can often escape their circumstances, while animals cannot.

To this extent, it is somewhat reasonable to conclude that we have a greater responsibility to animals than to humans, especially when the human whose welfare is at stake has a presumed obligation to see to their own preservation.
In this sense, we are the shepherds of animals, while other humans are assumed to be their own shepherds.
So while the tendency is understandable, it overlooks certain things.

Humans are animals, too, with greater capabilities than most, but still, subject to many of the same forces of nature as any other animal, and similar limits when it comes to their ability to change these circumstances.

While it might be comforting to assume that humans can do something about the obstacles that they face, it is often the case that small, seemingly petty factors can combine to force humans into a corner that they cannot get out of.
So, those who reserve their sympathy for animals might be well-advised to reconsider their priorities when it comes to the suffering of an individual, helpless human.
Because if a helpless animal is deserving of pity, and help, a helpless human, who is ultimately just another suffering animal,  is deserving of this, as well.
It makes no sense to respond to the suffering of one animal, and ignore the suffering of another who is equally, if not more, worthy of empathy and help.

Do you listen to audiobooks?

Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, listening to audiobooks can be a comparable if not more pleasant experience for many types of readers.
The benefits of listening to an audiobook, is that the reader can engage with a story at a good pace.
Some people are not as fast as readers as others, and notably may struggle to read depending on the contents of the story.
Others simply do not like holding a book, and would rather listen as they go through their daily tasks.
Listening is seen as a passive ability, as many are skilled at doing so while they engage in other activities such as driving, or even while exercising.

Listening also has the benefit of engaging a person into the setting of the story, as a good audiobook narrator is skilled at voicing the characters and also at setting the background and surroundings facing the characters.
Reading, while more active and requiring more concentration than listening, can be a more involved and personal activity than listening.
Readers can control their pace, and even take notes on areas in the book that they may wish to look into more or take further time to understand.
They can go back on what they read to see the characters under new contexts and information.
A reader, can also dictate how a character sounds, as listening to an audiobook sets that choice for the listener, who may or may not agree with the narrator's choice.
In my opinion, I prefer reading over listening to an audiobook.

While good audiobook narrators can add to the experience of a book, they are not able to be the definite choice for the author's characters, much less how I can picture the characters in their tone, dialect, and even inflection.

For me to get immersed, I have to chose my own pace for engaging in the story, taking the time to pause the story if I want to think more in depth about what has happened, or to connect it with other thoughts I may have.
An audiobook while it can be paused, will always move a constant pace dictated by the narrator.
Sometimes, I may show excitement or a strong interest to continue reading into the plot, reading faster to see what happens next to the characters.
Other times, I slow down to absorb all the information of the book's pages, to better understand what happens next in the book.
Ultimately I enjoy being able to address the story in ways that an audiobook cannot offer based on the strengths and weaknesses of both mediums.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?
Would you be surprised to hear that a study found that research subjects were more upset by stories of a dog beaten by a baseball bat than of an adult similarly beaten?
Or that other researchers found that if forced to choose, 40 percent of people would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist.
Why do you think many people are more empathetic toward the suffering of animals than that of people?
In your opinion, is it wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering?
Why do you think so?
In my opinion, being outraged about what goes through the heads of others is an unproductive way to do activism.
At the end of the day, it's not about what people think, it's about what they do.
While 40 percent of people may have said they would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist, it's another matter entirely what they would do in real life if faced in that situation.
The fact is, most people don't want to think about the suffering of others.
at all, whether they're human or animal or even a plant.
Humans are emotional and sympathetic creatures, with a vibrant capacity to feel pain; thus, we will often do anything to avoid those feelings of pain.

It's important to recognize that it can often be easier for a human to ruminate on the suffering of an animal as opposed to the suffering of a fellow human, because the animal is more distant to us and therefore harder to empathize with completely.
This doesn't necessarily speak to any given human's true morality, but rather their emotional coping mechanisms when faced with difficult moral questions.
The question of whether it's wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering is a fallacious one.
In fact, activists can care about multiple causes at once; it's not a zero-sum game.
Much in the same way that somebody can care about ending homelessness and ending racism, somebody else can care about protecting animals and protecting humans.
There's never anything wrong with caring, because caring about something does not preclude the possibility of caring about other things, whether they're 'worthy' causes or not.
Suggesting that one group (or species, as it were) is more important and worthy than another is simply a way to divide people who could otherwise be driven to unite over the same cause.
Instead of a world where people have to choose between animals and humans, why not a world where everybody cares about both?
Animals and humans are both worthy of our empathy, and it's important to recognize that.
Life itself is precious, and we should all be working together to protect it.

While 'working together' may not necessarily mean volunteering hands-on at a farm or attending the same pro-rights protest, it does mean respecting the decisions that each individual makes about where to devote their time, energy and compassion.
Our job as activists isn't to spy over the shoulder of our neighbors, waiting for them to slip up or have the wrong priorities, but to support each other in the causes that we all care about.
There's nothing wrong with caring about both animals and people too, because at the end of the day, the most important thing is that we care at all.

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?

Cody J. McDavis brings up interesting points and reasons for his stance against paying athletes.

For participating in such sports, athletes have to juggle various obligations, including their education.

At the same time, their focus lies on getting better at their sport, striving to improve to be the best they can be.

cDavis also argues that his stance for keeping things the way they are would not hurt fans, university, and alumni.

All together, this compromises the perseverance of a team, which lowers their appeal to their fans, and the prestige of the university.
Paying for college athletes is a small price to pay for the contributions they give to a university, and should be considered due to the positive effects it bestows on the athletes themselves.
McDavis is correct that paying athletes can lead to a discrepancy in how athletes are paid, causing a bidding war that is costly for universities to participate in and to maintain.

Athletes would realize their options in a free market.

Riku asked?

How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
Have you had any experience with dating?
Have you ever used dating apps?
If so, what has it been like for you?
If not, why not?
How do you think technology -- like apps, Netflix, social media and texting -- affects dating and relationships?
In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions?
How so?
In my opinion, dating apps have revolutionized dating.
In fact, I think they have had a very dramatic effect on social behavior, in general.
People are constantly on their phones, messaging each other.
That's not all dating apps at work, but dating behavior is a significant part of text messaging.
Dating apps have brought a lot of people into the dating world, that otherwise wouldn't have found their way in.
It's been great for everyone.
Lonely people are stepping back out into the world, and people who have always been outgoing have found a new, better outlet.
It's opened up a lot of possibilities.
I have used these apps myself, probably most of them.
I've had some great dates and some not so great dates.
Every one of them was a learning experience, in which I found something about myself that I hadn't previously been aware of.
These experiences have given me more confidence in my ability to communicate with strangers, and they've also improved my ability to socialize on a personal level.
I feel like I'm a better conversationalist, in general, as a result of my using dating apps to meet some new, random people.
The idea of meeting up with a stranger, about whom you know very little, can be daunting.
However, if you can get over that initial hurdle, then I think you'll find yourself having some great conversations with people.
Even situations where the dating doesn't work out can be socially fruitful.
I have a very good friend, we talk just about every day, who I met on a dating app.
We didn't continue to date, but we continued to talk.
We found that our friendship was missing from our lives, even though we were completely unaware of its possibility before meeting on a dating app.
Neither of us would have thought to reach out or see the other person, in any other context, even though we lived in the same place and had similar interests.
Dating apps have allowed me to meet a new friend who has likely had a deeper impact on my life than many of my true loves have.
I find a lot of upside to dating apps, and very few downsides.
Most of the downside to the apps would be if a person is very impatient, and doesn't feel comfortable around other people.
These apps only really require one thing of users, something that all participants need to have in common, and that is the ability to keep an open mind and be patient with oneself and others.
This is something that not everyone knows how to do, but once it is learned, it leads to new social connections with people, which can lead to a happier life.
I recommend that everyone who is looking to meet new people try a dating app, at least once.
Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?

Audiobooks are a useful way for people to gain access to books and literature they otherwise would not have access to, especially for those for whose mobility is limited, such as the elderly or people with physical disabilities.

In addition, they are helpful for people who are more time constrained than others, who do not possess the time or energy to read or, even for those that find it is easier and more convenient to listen to an audio book than to read the same book.
Those are all the advantages present in audiobooks, but if one wants to go further, there are some smaller but none-the-less important advantages.
For audiobooks are also more accessible by those who are illiterate as well as those who cannot read as fast as is required to follow along with a print book.
They are a good way for people to entertain and occupy themselves, and potentially learn more about a topic.
More people can hear an audiobook at a given time, which can open up discussion and potential further engagement with one another.
And most importantly, it is a gateway to literature for those who may not have access to the written word, or who might not enjoy reading as much.
For audiobooks need not to compete with the concept of reading, for they are a good complement for it that is accessible and available to many.
Just as audiobooks have advantages that worth considering, so do print books.
When reading, a person can set their own pace and decide for themselves how long to spend with the book, not having to worry about listening time.

In addition, they can become more invested in the literature, as reading makes the person more able to picture the events of the story, and even gives the reader greater input in how the story is read, as audiobooks have set narrators that voice the characters and events of the story.
For me, these are appealing benefits that draws me more to reading, than to listening to an audiobook.
That isn't to say as mentioned I would discourage the use of audiobooks for myself nor for others, just that if given the choice and time, I would find reading more enjoyable.
That is the critical aspect of both audiobooks and written literature, that ideally both should be available as a choice for people all around the world.
They both provides benefits and drawbacks that the other lacks, and I feel they can coexist without competition.
I think the two main choices will boil down to the preferences of the user, and they ultimately have to decide which works best for them at any given point in their life.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?

Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, no, we are not being bad citizens by not watching the news.

Just paying attention to what's going on in our environment will do just fine.

Surely avoiding this charade does not make someone a bad citizen.
aying attention and being connected to our communities alone will do a lot to keep our citizens informed.

Engaging with current event can be more helpful on a local level, for example if you are helping feed people in your community because of a tragedy.

All in all, I'd say people shouldn't be worried about not keeping up with the news.
There seem to be more bad effects from it than good and there are other ways to stay informed.
So, no.
We aren't bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news.

More than this?'

'Why are you still here?'

Where?

'Why are you so interested in them?'

I wish I had done that when I was a child.'

Something that was a part of her memory, but not.

Me too.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
What is a sport?
Is it a personal quest for achievement?
Hardly.
A sport is a business, and its purpose is to make money, pure and simple.
A sport gets played because it makes money for the owners and players.
Nowhere in the calculation of profit does it consider the risk to the participants.
As long as the public will buy tickets, watch on TV, buy sports apparel, cheer them on as heroes and call their names from the stands, anything goes.
he owners do not care whether their employees are alive or dead, so long as they make money.
The idea that society owes a duty of protection to athletes who are budding millionaires, and choose their sport voluntarily, is quaint.
Although some may expect them to avoid activities that may result in their premature death, it is not our duty.
Capitalism is amoral, money talks, and ethics fall by the wayside.
When we see a wealthy 23-year -ld pextreme slorts payer being carried on an air stretcher after rupturing a disk in his back, we shrug and wait for the next match.
If the player is cured, you can bet they will be right back in the arena.
And if he is forced into retirement, then just wait for the movie and book deals.
rensome sports too dangerous to play?
By what standards could this be even determined?
The players are earning a living, and they may be willing to risk their lives, for better or worse.
And the point of sports is to push limits and boundaries.
Without risk, there is no sport.
As long as there is a demand for high-risk athletes, there will be someone willing to take the chances.
And that demand shows no sign of abating.
So long as profits exceed the risks, the high-risk sports will persist.
And we should remember that hardly anything is safe anyway.
How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
Have you had any experience with dating?
Have you ever used dating apps?
If so, what has it been like for you?
If not, why not?
How do you think technology -- like apps, Netflix, social media and texting -- affects dating and relationships?
In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions?
How so?
In my opinion, and my experience, dating apps are a mixed bag.

On the one hand, they provide a way to meet people who you might not otherwise meet, but on the other, they might end up causing you to meet people who you really don't want to meet and would otherwise avoid.
On the good side when it comes to dating apps, they can be a relatively safe way of sizing up your dating options.

On the bad side, though, they can expose you to risk, by exposing you to people who might be dangerous or otherwise not good for you, and enabling those people to disguise their true nature until it's too late, and you 've already met them in person.
Netflix also has its good and bad sides.
One of the benefits of Netflix is that it allows you to watch a lot of movies and TV shows that you might not otherwise have seen, and that might facilitate getting to know more about your partner.

However, Netflix can also be a bad thing, because it can be a distraction from spending time with your partner, and it can also be a bad thing if you end up getting recommendations that one or the other of you don't like, and would otherwise avoid.
Texting, similarly, has both good and bad sides.
A benefit of texting is that it can be a relatively convenient way of communicating with a current or potential partner because it's not as immediate as talking on the phone or in person.
But a pitfall of this, is that it can lead to misunderstandings and miscommunications, and can also be a way of avoiding talking to your partner in person.
So, texting can either be a good or bad thing, depending on how it's used, and the specific circumstances of the relationship.

Personally, I haven't found dating apps, Netflix, or texting to be of much use in dating, but many of my friends and acquaintances have had very different experiences, and some have even met long term partners, or even spouses, through these means.
I guess like anything else, these are all tools.
They can do certain things, but it is ultimately up to the user to decide how they will be used, and whether they will be used for good or ill.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?

People need to realize that everything has a limit.

You shouldn't risk your life for the sake of winning.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, we should definitely be worried about screen time during the pandemic.
The evidence is clear: Screens are bad for us.
We are already seeing the negative effects of screen time on our children.
I know that my daughter Harper is glued to her iPad and she's only 7 years old, turning 8 soon next Valentine's Day.
I am worried about the effects of screen time on her brain development.
Of course, I'm usually too preoccupied with my own life to really monitor Harper's screen time to the T, but I do know that she's on her iPad for hours at a time.
Sometimes she'll even fall asleep with it in her hands.
When I ask her to put it down, she'll say, 'But Mommy, I'm almost done.'

Obviously I don't want her to be on her iPad for hours at a time, but I also don't want to be the kind of parent who is constantly telling my child what she can't do, since saying 'no' all the time is just not a good parenting strategy.
So far, I've been able to strike a balance between the two, but I'm not sure how much longer I can keep it up.
That's because during COVID, Harper's school went fully virtual, meaning that she's now spending all day on her iPad.
I mean, some of that time is obviously spent on actual learning, but I'm sure that there's a lot of time spent on mindless entertainment as well.
The thing is, is that I know that Harper is not the only child who is spending hours on her iPad.
I know that there are many other children who are spending more time on their iPads than they should be.
But there is so much more to life and to childhood than just sitting on your iPad all day.
When I was young, I spent a lot of time on my Game Boy, but I also played outside with my friends and I read books.
Moreover, I was a very social child and I had a lot of friends.
I loved meeting new people and I loved being around other kids.
On weekends, I would go to the mall with my friends and we'd hang out in the food court.
Now, I'm a little concerned because Harper is just glued to her iPad all day.
She really enjoys watching movies, and her favorite right now is Moana.
She also likes watching her favorite TV shows, which are mostly cartoons.
Ultimately, if I let her, Harper could spend all day on her iPad.
I don't want my seven year old daughter to be a social recluse.
And I definitely don't want her to be a couch potato, since that could negatively effect her health.
What happened to the days when kids played outside?
Every time I suggest to Harper that she go outside and play, she says, 'But Mommy, I'm almost done.'
Or sometimes I ask Harper if she wants to go to the park with me and she says, 'But Mommy, I'm watching a movie.'
Frankly, this doesn't seem to bode well for her future social life.
So I've decided I need to be much more vigilant about Harper's screen time.
That's not to say that I'm going to be a helicopter parent and constantly monitor Harper's screen time.
After all, I recognize that screen time is a necessary part of life.
And screen time is not all bad.
For example,  I think that screen time can be a great educational tool.
One game Harper really enjoys is called 'Math Bingo.'
She's learning math while playing the game.
And she's learning to read while playing 'Sesame Street.'
But at the same time I just really don't want to go down a rabbit hole with Harper where she's just sitting on her iPad all day.
Growing kids need to be active and they need to be social.
So this is where I come out on this issue, and I'm sure that there are many other parents out there who feel the same way.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, audiobooks are every bit as good as reading a book, and possibly superior to reading in some respects.

For starters, audiobooks are useful when driving, strolling in the park, cooking, cleaning, or doing any other activity that requires you to be able to see what you 're doing rather than focusing on a a book.

Books offer no corresponding advantage, as the main activity that audiobooks might prevent, listening to music or other audio, is something that would also prevent the level of focus required to read a book.
That brings up another advantage of audiobooks, the fact that they not only free up our eyes, but don't require the same level of focus that reading does.

It's possible to attempt to read a book, and end up unable to follow what's going on and getting distracted and losing your place, while with an audiobook, you might well be able to make your way through the recording without getting distracted, and still retain what's going on in the story.
Audiobooks also better engage the imagination.

The sound of the words being read aloud, is immeasurably more evocative than their appearance on a page, and it's also the case that, when using sound rather than sight to engage our mental processes, we tend to engage them more fully, using both sides of our brain to process the resulting data, rather than just the one side that reading hard copy books activates.

There's also the fact that audiobook narrators are often good enough that they can add an extra dimension to the story, or just their reading voice in itself is worth listening to, which can not only elevate a decent story, but also enhance the experience of reading something that's otherwise uninteresting by itself.
Audiobooks are also accessible in areas where books may not be available.

Not everyone has a tablet, and many people attempting to read e-books on public transit or on trains experience difficulties like motion sickness, while doing so, either due to the glare on their screen or just the general inconvenience of reading while moving.
Also, audiobooks enable us to tune out distractions while listening to them on headphones in public settings like mass transit, whereas books lack the ability to do that.
In closing, audiobooks are in no regard worse than books, and in many ways, better.

If I were forced to choose one over the other, I'd have to say that, for me, as well as most people, the myriad extra benefits of listening to audiobooks would more than compensate for any loss that the lack of a printed page could entail.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In some ways, many if not all sports are selfish to pursue.
The pursuit of any sport requires dedication, patience and often sacrifice to achieve one's goals, which includes prestige and reputation.
The top athletes are revered by many, but their actions do not necessarily benefit others directly.
Rather, many athletes serve as sources of inspiration, to motivate others to achieve their goals and overcoming obstacles, even if it isn't regarding the same sport or activity.
When it comes to high risk sports, the cathlete puts time and effort to train and hone their abilities, to meet with exceedingly high demands that are associated with those kind of sports.
Like other sports, the end results or reasons for why such people would do high risk sports deemed dangerous are primarily self-serving.
It is often for fame and prestige, while some do it to prove themselves that they can.
It is often about pushing the limits of what is possible, and leaving behind a legacy.
Those people that do break the boundaries of the sports are often revered by many, who hear their achievements and see what can be achieved with effort and time.
In that cases, pursuing those sports have indirect benefits to others who hear of such achievements.
Many can be inspired by tales of people who climb supposedly unscaleable mountains, or people who despite the risk of some sports, were able to break world records.
Pursuing those sports are a conscious action people take, who are often well aware of the stakes and dangers found in the sport.
In terms of what a person finds is too dangerous to pursue, that lies in the person and how they perceive said sport.

Some might perceive mountain climbing as being too dangerous and decline to even attempt it, while others will put in all of the effort, spending years getting better at it, to accomplish feats and impressive displays of prowess.
What a person deems is dangerous, might be doable to another person.

Thus I doubt that there will be a sport that exists in the world that would be considered by all as too dangerous to do, especially since high risk sports have been around for so long, with people always finding a way to up the ante of the sport.
The important thing to note is that the athletes and participants of high risk sports need to be aware of the dangers, and that they take the necessary precautions to minimize failure.
Through that, they can not only get better at the sport, but achieve their hopes and aspirations regarding the sport itself.

How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
Have you had any experience with dating?
Have you ever used dating apps?
If so, what has it been like for you?
If not, why not?
How do you think technology -- like apps, Netflix, social media and texting -- affects dating and relationships?
In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions?
How so?
In my opinion, technology has affected dating and relationships in both a positive and negative way.
As far as positives go, dating apps make it easier to see a wide selection of potential people you can 'swipe right' on, so most times you're more likely to find a potential match.
This gives you a much wider dating pool than you would have in the past, and increases the opportunities of finding a potential mate.

When it comes to something like Netflix's positive effect on dating, the amount of access to shows that appeal to all different tastes makes it easier to find something that is compatible with both your interests, and those of your potential mate.
It's minor, but it doesn't hurt to be able to watch something you already have in common.

The positives of social media related to dating and relationships come from the fact that you can socialize online, and develop your feelings for someone in a virtual way by sharing photos, blogs, photos.
In this way, it's possible to get to know someone , and maybe even fall in love, without ever meeting them face to face.
The positive effects of texting on dating and romance are that, unlike over the phone, there is little pressure to answer or make conversation.
This allows for a lot more space and privacy, which many find much more comfortable when it comes to dating.
Of course, these things also have their negatives.
Dating apps can increase the likelihood of being matched with someone you aren't compatible with as well as someone you are, which can make dating frustrating and disappointing.
Netflix can make it so easy to just chill and watch something with someone that you don't put in as much effort into making conversation, or truly getting to know them.
Social media can make it easier to keep up false appearances, which can lead to lying to your partner and hiding things.

And texting makes it easier to hide your feelings and intentions from a significant other, which can be damaging to your relationship when those feelings and intentions rear their head in real-life settings.
I have not used dating apps, but as far as social media and texting goes, I find them discouraging in terms of meeting someone.
Then again, I had the same issues with traditional dating in the past, so I suppose that's just me.
I think ultimately that dating is still dating, and relationships are still relationships, no matter what changes one might make to them with technology.
People who had an easy time with dating in the past, still will, and those, like me, who have found it a struggle, will continue to struggle, regardless of apps or Netflix.

Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, there are many pros and cons to paying college athletes.
I personally feel that it is less problematic to not pay college athletes and for this reason i would side with not paying them.
However, i think the root of the problem just comes with the large amount of money schools make off of these college athletes.
NCAA is one of the highest payed organizations in the world, and much of this is because they dont have to pay their athletes.
This makes people refer to the athletes almost like they are being taken advantage of.

I understand the perspective of the athlete being taken advantage of, however they are still given the platform to demonstrate their skills, and also given the opportunity to play in front of large crowds and meet tons of people, and build a following on social media.
Many perks come with being a college athlete aside from just possibly being paid.
The free tuition is nice for the athlete, however i dont know how much paying the athletes would be helpful.
Would they be paid based off of talent, or just a flat fee?
If it was a flat fee, the athletes would probably want more anyway if they were the star players.
I am personally a former college football player as well, and I just feel that it is not necessary to pay the players.
I think it would be nice to have more in place for the athletes, but not necessarily just a pay check.
I know there are some athletes who can barely afford college and food while being there.
This is unexceptable to me if they are part of a team making that much money for the university.
I would treat it like a job and simply provide the best working conditions for athletes that do a lot to help the school run.
No student athlete at all should have to worry about getting food to eat, or having a place to stay.
I think this is a good compromise to the problem.
Using some of the money to give back to athletes instead of giving athletes the freedom to spend on whatever they wish.

I am for the side of not paying athletes because i think there are too many variables associated with the amount you would pay them, and it is also sort of starting a bidding process right out of high school.
College would almost be like the pros in a way if you could get paid like a professional athlete.
If anything i think a flat fee would be most fair for everyone who was a part of the actual team.
This way, nobody is glorified in the amount that they are paid.
This would literally create powerhouses and the same schools would win every year just because they have the most money.
I think it would be a good idea to have a stipend for the athletes as well, just to make sure that they are able to make ends meet.
Just more structured types of payment that is more equal to all of the players on the team.
There are simply too many downsides of paying each player based off of their value, and i dont think it would be something that would be easy to bounce back from for the NCAA.
All this being said, the NCAA has to stop being stingy with their money and simply treat the athletes better.
If this was the case, this would not even be a discussion.
In conclusion however, i feel that the NCAA should not pay college athletes, at least in the same way pro players are paid.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, the reasoning that existed before the pandemic should still apply.
Namely that screen time should be monitored, and that limiting your screen time is best for both mental and physical health.
The science shows that too much screen time contributes to obesity, diabetes and hypertension.
It can cause eye strain, disrupt your mental state, and alter your sleep patterns.
That last one is very important, as uninterrupted sleep is an absolute requirement for fighting viruses and to speed up our healing responses.
If there is one good thing that has come out of the pandemic it is increased awareness of health, and a new focus on maintaining and improving health.
Limiting screen time is an important part of this.
This is not to say that we should give up on screen altogether.
They are an important tool for work efficiency, social connection, and overall entertainment.
The main point is a balance must be found.
Do you think you're spending too much time on your screen?
Then you probably are.
Like anything else, technology can become excessive and unhealthy if not properly moderated.

Exploring other alternatives in cases where screen related activities have taken over can help you learn where screens are essential to you, and where you could give them up (or use them less) for alternatives.
In short, studies have shown that screen time can affect you physical and mental health, so treat screen time like you would anything else that can affect you health.
Monitor and examine how it effects you.
List the benefits and negatives , and you will be able to discover what you can do to integrate screen use into your life while minimizing any health effects.
And keep up to date with new studies and new technologies; you may learn things which cause you to re-evaluate your current usage.
And above all else; don't rely on screentime activities to provide you with everything (work, entertainment, social interaction).
Variety is always the healthiest choice.

econd, you have to be able to listen to the book at a certain pace.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, we should be worried about excessive screen use.
The key word there is excessive.
There is nothing wrong with using a laptop or a cell phone.
The issue becomes when we rely too heavily on those devices.
When instead of socializing with others and spending time with humans, we'd rather stay on our phone or laptop.
We had to rely on our screens during the pandemic.
I think a lot of us would have went crazy without that because we couldn't really socialize with others.
We couldn't go out.
We had to stay inside and be as safe as possible.
That means that our only way of entertainment was to watch television, use the internet, play video games, etc.
There is obvious value in screen time.
We can get so much information from the internet nearly instantly.
Screens can help us get from point A to point B via GPS.
The key to screen time just like everything else in life is balance.
If we are using our screens too much it can have a negative effect on our social life as well as our physical health.
Too much screen time can hurt our eyes.
I don't think this is an all or nothing topic.
We can use our screens and embrace technology while not relying on them 24 hours a day.
There are already trackers on our phone that show us how often we use our phone.
How often we pick the phone up.
Our average screen time each week.
We can use those statistics to see if we're using our phones too much.
If we are, it's pretty simple...have some willpower and cut down on screen time.
After all, social relationships will always be more valuable than anything you can find on the internet.
Use your screens and enjoy your life.
But make sure screens and devices aren't priority number one.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, whether a sport is reasonable or not depends on the purpose, goals and motives of the participants.

Those who participate in the sport purely for recreation or adrenaline may promote a rationale for doing dangerous activities like skydiving, rock climbing or ski jumping, But what is the goal of the sport?
What defines winning?
What defines losing?
How do the rules determine what's fair and what's unfair?

It all seems a bit pretentious, even if it's a thrill -- not to mention expensive -- to hurtle oneself off a high cliff or summit if there is not a clearly-defined way of doing it well or poorly, or right or wrong.

But if the goal of the sport is to achieve a specific outcome that has not yet been achieved, as in trying to travel farther or higher, that increases the risk of someone getting hurt or damaging something.
Reckless and irresponsible behavior is condoned if the consequences are not likely to extend beyond the individual(s) who are participating.
Is that selfish when the sport can clearly be categorized as dangerous?
I think so.
Reckless behavior goes against the concept and principles in sport, which is honor, integrity, fairness and respect.
Acting responsibly is something that should be frowned up, especially in competition.
Sports teach much in the way of values, or principles that can help us to determine how we should live our lives.
That is why we should aim to label activities as sports only if they promote or sustain the value of sports.
Otherwise, it's just a dangerous game.
Dangerous games have consequences that must be faced, and I don't want those to taint the idea of what sports are.

The single-player campaign is centered around this objective, and the player will have to fight his way through numerous levels (most of which are on-rails) while playing as the protagonists of various missions.ut of Exile makes use of the standard FPS control scheme, namely the WASD keys for movement and mouse aiming; however, players can choose between a first-person view and a third-person view, although the third-person one is only available while using some weapons.

Why do you think the way you do?
In this day in age, citizens all around the world are potentially subjected to a significantly higher amount of information, than citizens that existed in the past.

For many in the past, it was not expected that one could know anything that was going on beyond their country or community, given the lack of technology such as the internet, social media, or even television and other types of viewing devices.

Traditional media in those eras, such as newspapers were often locally controlled, and opinionated from a particular point of view that did not encompass all the perspectives and opinions prevalent in the world at the time.
While people could be argued to be better informed of the local events that would affect them, today I believe people are much more informed of what is occurring all around the world.
As a result of various factors, we might feel we have a greater responsibility to keep up all types of events, even ones that occur internationally alongside with local and national events.

For most people have obligations to account for, in addition to taking the time to get informed and stay up to date with current news and events.
Some have less time to keep up with the news, spending a lot of their waking time at work and other obligations.
Others can have more free time to stay informed, which in too can lead to other actions such as political engagement and activism.
The citizens with less time on their hands to keep up with the news are not necessarily worse than those that do, nor would I consider them bad citizens.

For this basic awareness people have coincides with the possibility they will spread what they know to others, and inform people of what events they are up to date with.
With the prevalence of technology, this means people will know about the news more readily, especially with the impact of social media in connecting people with relevant information.
This will lead to action, as there will be people who can do something about certain events, whether it is voting, protesting, and much more.
It is vital that people stay informed about the news, but due to time constraints for most, they might not keep up with all the news all the time.

Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, if a university or college is profiting off of a student athlete, the student athlete should be paid monetarily and not via scholarship.
A student athlete getting paid would not the economy of universities.
The amount that these schools make off of the student athletes is incredible.
We're talking about millions and in some case billions of dollars and the student athletes don't see a cent of that.
I do understand the point that student athletes would become a bidding war for universities that have a lot of capital.
I don't see that as any difference than free agency in sports.
Typically the highest bidder will win but there are some cases where an athlete wants to be close to home or takes a hometown discount.
At the very least, the student athlete should have to weigh those options.
The easy way to solve that issue as well is simply to limit the amount that a student athlete can make.
$250,000 is a fantastic salary for a student athlete and is life changing money for any 18 to 22 year old.
You can put a specific criteria on the salary such as maintaining a 2.0 GPA each semester or their salary is forfeited or at the very least a portion is.
This allows there to be fair competition between the universities and a school like Alabama won't be able to simply outbid a school like Syracuse.
Student athletes are working as a full time athlete and a full time student.
Shouldn't they be paid for their efforts?
What happens if a student athlete gets both a academic and an athletic scholarship?
That student is punished if they get a full ride for both categories.
They are entitled to 2X the scholarship amount and instead just get one scholarship amount.
The business of college athletics has been a scam for way too long.
Student athletes have been exploited by universities for far too long.
You have coaches like Clemson's Dabo Swinney saying that student athletes shouldn't be paid and that he'd retire if they did.
Well, a bill was passed that allows student athletes to get paid for their imagine and likeness.
Did Swinney retire?
Of course not.
He makes upwards of 10 million dollars a year.
Imagine that.
A coach making 10 million dollars a year while his players make absolutely nothing.
Again, a scenario where most logical and reasonable people will look at and say 'that is unfair.'
The only people who will say that it's fair are the people that are making tons of money off of those student athletes.
Luckily, more and more people who have power have seen this issue and have acted in the student's favor.
I look forward to more laws and bills being passed that allows student athletes to get their fair share of money.

What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?
What stereotypical characters in books, movies or television shows make you cringe and why?
Would you ever not watch or read something because of its offensive portrayal of someone?
In my opinion, stereotypes by themselves are not always harmful, as they are simply a shortcut that people make when they do not have enough information about an individual.
However, even though they are not intended to be harmful, they often can be, especially to the person who is being judged.

I cringe when I see a character that is a stereotype because it makes me feel like the author is lazy., but I also feel that this use of stereotyping might end up being harmful to the group that the author is writing about.

For example, if an author writes about black youths who end up committing crimes, this would further strengthen society's expectations that young black males are violent, and this will lead others not to trust them.
Clearly, this is not right, because crime comes from poverty, not from race.
I wwas fortunate in life to have been born a white male, which gives me definite advantages.
However, if I was a member of a minority group, I ould nprefer ot wto atch or read something that is offensive to me, because I would feel like the author is being disrespectful to me.
I would also feel that I was rewarding this conduct on the part of authors and screenwriters, which would further encourage it.
As a member of the majority, though, I do still cringe when I see minority groups portrayed in an insensitive, stereotypical fashion on TV, in movies, and to a lesser extent in books.
This not only harms the group as a whole, but it also affects individual actors.

When there are no roles available for minority actors except for those that perpetuate stereotypes, these actors are either left without opportunities, or they have to betray their morals in order to keep working.
If people were more apt to reject stereotypes, these difficult decisions would not have to be made.
Stereotypes do not always have to be negative, however.
Someone might assume that a young Asian person is smart, especially at math, or that someone who wears glasses is a good student.

I generally do not have a severe negative reaction to these stereotypes, because I do not see any acute harm that comes from them, but they are still lazy.
One should not assume that the circumstances of one's birth have any impact on their character or their abilities.
After all, if you automatically assume that an Asian student is going to be the best in the class, aren't you also assuming that the other students are naturally inferior, because of their race?
ISo, in summary,  do not think that it is wrong to have a stereotype,.b This is something that happens automatically within our brains, and we can't really stop these thoughts from popping up.
Bt I think that it is wrong to judge someone based on a stereotype that either comes from within, or that we have picked up from society at large.

Not only do stereotypes lead to negative judgments against others, which sometimes have real-world consequences, but they also prevent people from enjoying the kinds of equal opportunities that all of us deserve.
The stereotype may be inevitable, but the prejudice that it leads to comes about by choice.
And that is a choice that no one should be making.

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).

They are the face of their schools, and they are the ones who put in the time and effort to make their schools successful.
This is also in addition to juggling courseloads, jobs, and other student activities.
Any other student working for the university would get paid, up to and including the mascot, so why not the actual athletes themselves?
The NCAA is a multi-billion dollar industry, and it is not paying its workers.
It's unfair to claim that paying athletes would cause financial issues for universities when those athletes bring in so much money in the first place.
Raising ticket prices to sporting events would be one way to make up for the money that would be paid to athletes, for example.
Another would be to pay athletes a standard wage much in the same way that other student staff are compensated; this would eliminate any risk of big universities buying star players.

If they will be paid for being in the big leagues, why not also pay them for the work that they do at a lower level?
The NCAA is a stepping stone for these athletes, and it is unfair to them to not compensate them for their performance and efforts.
Even in athletics, the principles of workers' rights still apply.
College athletes are not just students; they are entertainers, professionals, public figures, and ultimately workers.
Their lives revolve around being in top physique so they can play for their universities the same way that major league players would.
For this reason, they should absolutely be compensated and held in the same regard as anybody else who performs services of value.
