Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news?
Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world?
Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all?
Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, someone who does not keep up with the news is not a bad citizen, but they cannot call themselves a good and responsible citizen either.
n other words, Ithink that everyone has some responsibility to know what is going on in the world, but I do not think that it is a requirement.
to call oneself a citizen.
The news ultimately affects all of us, whether directly, or indirectly through the political process.

We cannot make good decisions without being informed, so I think that it is important for any responsible citizen to follow events in the news and to understand the historical underpinnings of events.

If one does not follow the news in the world, and does not therefore understand what is happening, they will be apt to make bad decisions that not only affect themselves, but could potentially be harmful for others as well.
Think of the people who refuse to listen to scientific fact about vaccines.
They are the reason why Covid-19 has not been controlled in the United States, despite the fact that we have ample access to vaccines.
This lack of information, or more seriously, abundance of false information, has been literally deadly to many.
However, I do not think that it is necessary for everyone to be a news junkie.
I think that it is important to be informed, but I do not think that it is necessary to know every detail of every story.
In fact, spending too much time concentrating on current events can actually be harmful in itself, since it would distract from other pursuits.
Getting too bogged down in the minutiae of up-to-the-minute events can also lead to a poor understanding of the events themselves, since one will not be able to step back and see the history.
One would not be seeing the forest because the trees are in the way, as the old saying goes.
My opinion of the news media is not strictly positive, though.
Media outlets, at best, chase ratings or (in the case of public broadcasting) donations from members, and this can lead them to focus on eye-catching reporting at the expense of important reporting.

Very few news outlets spend much time on budgetary concerns in government, or distant ethnic tensions, because readers are not interested, but if this information was pushed to the forefront, it could be beneficial to everyone.
In addition, we cannot pretend that the news media is impartial and unbiased.
All persons are biased toward a certain viewpoint, and this bias can become entrenched when journalists have to please college professors and later editors who all tend to feel the same way.

When alternative media outlets pop up, they end up pushing brainless conspiracy theories instead of giving fact-based rebuttals to biases at other sources, because this is what their viewers want to hear.
And even when they act responsibly, highly partisan news sources often take an extreme position, even when they back it up with facts and evidence.

In conclusion, I think that everyone has some responsibility to be informed about the world around them, but I do not think that it is necessary (or even wise) for them to spend the majority of their time on the news.
In addition, they need to be skeptical about what they hear in the news media, but even more skeptical about people who claim that the media are always wrong.
Finally, responsible citizens need to not only follow the news, but also try to get a deeper understanding of what led to current events.
Some of the time spent reading the newspapers would be better spent reading a book that chronicles the full story of a recent, or current, event.

We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?

In my opinion, the screen usage of a typical human have significantly increased over the years, and I do not want to be hypocritical, but right now, I think I'd rather read a book than a newspaper or watch TV.
My dependence for screens is very much like a drug.
I do not know what do with myself one day when my computer broke and I needed to purchase a part and it has not arrived yet.
I was going crazy.
There was more to life than checking my e-mail every few minutes or browsing the Web for background information to support a presentation.
Sure, having access to phones and computers all the time has its benefits.

For one, there are plenty of ways this digital age allows us to communicate with people across the globe, and there are also lots of ways we are able to educate people without the need for one on one contact, specially during the time of the pandemic, when it is mandatory to keep distance from other people.
But it's definitely ruining my life.
The same way how drugs overused can ruin someone's life when they're addicted to it, overly involved in computer, video games or other applications is the same.
There was nothing interesting to do in my house, nor in my neighborhood, or anywhere in the town, and I became totally dependent for my entertainment.
I did not want to communicate with people, because there was nothing to talk about and I was tired of it.
My social intelligence and how I connect with people have become a bit damaged, only because I was left alone with this computer and now, I never know what to do with myself when I'm out in the open.
It's very scary.
So yeah, while I do not want humanity to go back to the Dark Ages, when there were no electrical devices invented, I do not think it will be a good idea for humanity to go through another Dark Age.
And there's no denying that having all the humanities' knowledge and information at your finger tips is not a bad thing.
But at the same time, aspects that you normally do not consider that's being damaged like social intelligence and the ability to remember things, are negatively impacted.
Our reliance to technology has to be limited at one point, not just because it is a good practice to do if you want to keep your life on track.
As for me, I will try my best to contact more people I know and if we can return to normal, possibly even go to the town once again.
Find more people to communicate with, and try to carefully pick and choose what technology, video games, programs or apps I decide to use.
Screen use will not go away any time soon, but we shouldn't be too dependent on them to the point it hurts our abilities to connect with other people.
Remember, technology was made to help us, and not to be addicted to.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, there are many potential downsides and benefits to the constant use of our devices, depending on their content, context and purpose.
For example, it's been linked to low social competence in younger kids, as a distraction from family bonding, and a risk factor for obesity.
However screen time also allows for younger kids to learn new things by using apps and using the internet.
Screen time simply needs to be used in moderation.
Social media is very similar.
There are pros and cons to everything but when you overuse something it becomes a negative.
There's a reason that if you overuse coffee, it'll make you feel anxious and irritable.
A cell phone or a tablet can work the same way.
It also can damage your eyes.
Screen time during the pandemic was on the rise simply because we all were stuck at home.
There wasn't much to do.
Screens probably kept us from going insane.
Imagine being stuck at home and not being able to use the internet or watch television.
What would people who live alone do?
Stare at a wall?
Screen time is beneficial to humans.
It allows us to have basically any information at our fingertips.
It allows us to relax and wind down.
It allows us to keep our mind off the problems and issues that we face on a daily basis.
It also allows us to keep in contact with our family and friends via FaceTime and texting.
In general I believe that screen time isn't a real issue for most of the population.
As long as you keep it in moderation and it isn't affecting your physical or mental well being, do what you enjoy in life.

If somebody doesn't care what is going on or doesn't want to know, that's fine.
But I think as a citizen, it's worthwhile to try and occasionally be informed.
I don't know that any one person can actually do anything to change the larger social issues, but I think it's worthwhile as a way to participate.

f you don't, though, I don't think you're doing anything wrong.

o you think that the things that are happening in the news are actually affecting your life or this society in any significant way?

Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, there's no need to pay athletes.
It will just cause a lot of issues that we can avoid.
Just because athletes shouldn't be paid doesn't mean that they don't deserve anything in return for playing.
They bring money to the school after all.
Maybe they could receive incentive in other ways.
They could get free boarding.
They could receive free meals.
Those things are smaller but it's something that wouldn't drastically take away from the money that the college has.
That money could be put to better use.
Sports will always be a large part of collegiate life.
That's just how it is.
We just have to figure out a way to realistically handle this.
I am optimistic that we will be able to find a solution that improves the college experience for everyone involved.
Maybe something could be set up to help with them getting recruited.
That is the end goal anyway.
To find a way to give them more exposure and get them recognized in a winning program.
That wouldn't cost anything.
It would just require colleges to get creative and work with recruiters in inventive ways.
I think this is less of an issue of if we should pay athletes.
We shouldn't.
This is more of an issue of if we should set up some sort of system that takes care of the athletes without money being involved.
That should be the goal.
We still want to allow the athletes to get something in return, it's just that money needs to be taken out of the equation.
By doing that we can make everyone happy.
That will end this debate and help to keep the integrity that colleges have in place.
That integrity is crucial because if that is gone what is left?

We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, we should worry about excessive screen time.
We have a whole generation growing up without knowing who their real friends are, or what a real relationship feels like to be friends with somebody.
It's so much easier to be mean to somebody on the other side of a screen, and then you can just 'unfriend' them.
ocial interaction is being lost, because people are spending more time just being on their screens and watching videos.
Kids are growing up without learning that they can share their feelings directly with a person.
It's all about, 'I'll send you a message, and we'll use texting and chatrooms instead.'
People are being held away at a distance, instead of being able to sit in the same room and talk to somebody.
t's a whole different way of socializing.

We're in the middle of what I worry is becoming a permanent societal isolation.
My mom went into a meeting with a school teacher who told her the kids aren't playing in the playground anymore.
They have these iPads, and they're at their own little table by themselves.
There's no crossing over and talking to each other, or hearing a different voice than their own.
They don't hear stories; they don't hear the sounds and smells.
They're growing up missing all those things.

I worry that the hearing and speech development of young children is being damaged, because they're not using their mouths or their ears to hear and understand the different sounds of real-life speech.

How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
Have you had any experience with dating?
Have you ever used dating apps?
If so, what has it been like for you?
If not, why not?
How do you think technology -- like apps, Netflix, social media and texting -- affects dating and relationships?
In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions?
How so?
In my opinion, all these things have done is further complicate the already complicated and awkward process of attempting to have some kind of romantic interaction with someone you are attracted to.

Since the dawn of time, people have managed to establish intimate relationships by meeting each other in real life, gradually learning to trust one another, and eventually being at the point to where they really want to begin a relationship with each other.
21st century technological developments have only added a layer of bizarre complexity to this process, and have further isolated people to the point where this process fails before it can even begin.
Dating apps are the greatest example of this.
I've used them, and the experience is not unlike playing online poker, or playing video games -- the main point of it is to kill time in lieu of having better things to do.

The way the time killing process works with them, is that, you open up the app, conveniently right around the time you would otherwise go to bed, and start swiping through dozens of unappealing or phony users until you find one or two that you like, and begin exchanging messages with them, which might then end in a flaky or disconnected face-to-face interaction, which might then end in a crappy date that doesn't lead to anything further, which then leads you back to the beginning with yet more profiles of people you don't have anything in common with, and who you don't really want to meet.
This does nothing to build a foundation of trust and rapport, and it does nothing to help people connect with each other.

Netflix is a mere time waster, it's much like going to a video store, only with thousands of titles rather than hundreds, few of which either you or a prospective partner will have any interest in watching, and the whole process is more likely to result in awkward silence and resentment over poor viewing choices, than a romantic connection.

Texting is very much the same way -- the only difference is that it sucks even more time out of your day, and takes more from your life, as you fail over and over to communicate with someone like a real human being, and wind up resorting to emoticons.

What all of these things have in common, beyond being ineffectual for dating or relationships, is that they are all means for some greedy corporate entity to make money, and ultimately if you build a real relationship, the money making will stop, so they have interest in facilitating relationships.
The best response is to ignore them all, and meet someone in the gym, library, a book store, coffee shop, or on a hiking trail somewhere.

Then, once you're in a relationship, you can rest satisfied, knowing that not only have you met someone you might spend the rest of your life with, you've also saved a ton of money in the process and helped to put Netflix out of business.

How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
Have you had any experience with dating?
Have you ever used dating apps?
If so, what has it been like for you?
If not, why not?
How do you think technology -- like apps, Netflix, social media and texting -- affects dating and relationships?
In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions?
How so?
In my opinion, based on ten years of using dating apps and similar technological gimmicks, I believe technology is improving dating.
Let's start with dating apps.
Before the advent of stuff like Tinder and Grindr, you had to go out to bars and clubs or to parties if you wanted to find someone with whom you were interested in dating.
The odds that you would meet someone you really liked were pretty slim, but still, you had to do it if you didn't want to be alone.
It also took a lot of time and effort, and frequently that time and effort was wasted.
Since the advent of apps, this is no longer the case.
You can do the same thing, with the added advantage that you can do it from the comfort of your own home, and you can do it whenever and wherever you want to.

I'm not sure that the odds of success are greater, but since it takes less effort, and since the result is substantially the same, you can find someone you like a lot more easily... and then talk to him or her without wasting energy and cutting into your schedule in the same way.
I could say similar things about Netflix.
Before Netflix and the like existed, you and your partner had to rent movies from the video store or go to the theater.
The selection was limited and it was often difficult to find something that both of you would enjoy.

It became a repetitive, frustrating ritual, going to the video store, looking at the shelves, putting stuff on hold, waiting for it to come in, then watching the movie and often feeling unsatisfied afterward.

Renting a bummer of a movie often led to arguments about whose fault it was for renting that title, and not finding stuff you both wanted led to arguing about how you should have gone to the theater instead.
With Netflix, you can still end up with bad movies, but the consequence is less severe, and most of the time, you can find something you both want... even if it's different stuff.
Texting, compared to prior methods of communicating, is superior in its speed and lack of pronouns.
It's quicker than a call, and it avoids the problem of people being on different schedules and talking at different times.
It is somewhat limited in what it can communicate, but in many cases, that's a plus, because it reduces arguments about what's being said and read into.
On the whole, it's made staying in touch with partners much easier and more enjoyable.
And that's kind of my take on all the 21st century innovations in dating.
They haven't fundamentally changed the things that you need to do to establish and maintain a relationship, but they have made doing all of those things easier and more convenient.
What could be wrong with that?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'

first of all, it would be a huge distraction for the players.

Just to get high profits, instead of focusing on spending money to make their schools better.
It would be like an open stock market for college athletes.

In your opinion, what are the most important things students should learn in school?
What is the most important thing you have learned in school?
How has this knowledge affected your life?
How do you think it will help your success in the future?
In my opinion, the most important things students should learn in school are how to get along with others, and how to be successful on the job.
Few people go on to pursue a job that requires a highly specific degree.
Most people just finish high school and get a job.
Because of that they really need to learn social skills first.
School forces you to be around people you may not like.
You are put into classes with people you may not know.
The more you learn how to get along with others the better off you will be.
That skill comes in handy when it's time to work.
You again will be surrounded by people you may not like and you'll need social skills to navigate the situation.
Second there's the job market.
School will show you what things you are interested in and good at.
You may learn that you are good at math so you feel comfortable getting an office job where you do paperwork.
On the other hand you may learn that you are better at working with people and serving them or being directly around them, such as in a doctor's office.
These things you learn in school show you what you'll be good at.
Obviously students need to learn the basic skills to get through life like learning English and basic math skills.
From there though it really comes down to just finding out your social skills and the things you enjoy doing.
School helps you with those things, it really opens your eyes to many choices so that you can choose the career that fits you and the one you will want to stick with.
Since most of us will not get a college degree it is important to realistically view school for what it is.
It's a chance to just learn about ourselves and use that to guide us through our work life as an adult.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, screen time is an important benchmark in how we are spending our time.
Whether or not there is inherent risk in what we do on our screens aside, spending too much time staring at a screen is physically unhealthy.
t's not just the eyes that suffer, it's the body.

Apps are available for all major platforms which can help us monitor our screen time.
I use Moment on my iPhone and it's a great way to keep track of how much time I spend on my phone.
With the information I'm provided, by the app, I am better able to manage my daily activities.
For instance, I can restrict my phone usage to a certain number of minutes, or hours, before taking a break to exercise, rest or do something else.
I find that when I'm keeping track of my time in a more detailed way, I am shocked by the amount of time I devote to staring at a screen.
also use a desktop app called Self Control to block certain websites for a set amount of time.
The pandemic is very difficult for everyone but if we can find any bright spots in the tragedy of this time period, I think we will find them in retrospect.
We are living through a difficult time, but it will help us to learn how to live better.

A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
College athletes are in many ways comparable to athletes older than them, that participate in professional leagues outside of colleges and universities.
Many of college athletes put in tremendous amount of effort and their time to improve their abilities, and to seek achievement of the sport of their choosing.

They still have educational obligations to meet apart from the demands of the sport, which in too can conflict with work demands if they hold one.
Having to juggle a variety of obligations in a day can be tiring and stressful, which impacts the performance of a college athlete much like any other type of athlete.

However, the college athletes that are not paid to the same degree as professional athletes like in the MLB, NFL, NHL, and much more will no doubt be subjected to much more stressors from the lack of finances.
The argument that college athletes should not be paid ithat is ased on the idea that the current system of scholarships and other benefits is enough.
is a flawed line of thinking.
That is assuming that college athletes like other students, don't accumulate debt through other expenses apart from the ones necessary to pay for their education.
Scholarships and other benefits are sufficient to pay for tuition and the cost of materials, but like other students, many of college athletes have other areas to attend to.
This includes living arrangements, food, hobbies, and much more than will be difficult to pay for with scholarships and other benefits, more so for some than others.

Paying them like other athletes will help them meet the demands of their finances as it relates to their education, personal life, and their sport.
The argument that paying college athletes would ruin the sport is also flawed., given that such a concept exist in professional leagues and other sports.
Universities benefit much from college athletes, more so from the ones that have high prestige, performance, and reputation.

The bidding wars and other excessive costs that universities pay for their athletes are in part of their own vocation, something that can be prevented through more regulation, and effecitvely the fair treatment of all college athletes for their efforts.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, as long as the activity in question is reasonably regulated and you choose to participate knowing the risks, then it should not be called too dangerous to be considered a sport.
There are risks involved in all sports--if you decide it's too dangerous and don't participate, then that's OK.
But if you are going to participate, you should know what risks there are.

I would much rather experience a risky and high-stakes sport, compete at it with others, than never have had the opportunity to do something that sometimes pushes me to my limitsIf an activity is putting people in a position where they are forced to engage in it by the government or a governing athletic organization, then I have a problem with it.
Some Eastern Asian and African countries come to mind, where athletes are occasionally compelled to compete.

There are recent stories of athletes being forced to compete despite a legitimate injury, and being punished if they don't, and even worse, having their families punished by their communities when they refuse.
In the western world, we want individuals to participate voluntarily, safely and with respect for rules, communities and nature.
For example, snorkeling at a tropical reef might be a relatively safe activity, but you better understand the dangers of rip tides and sharks.
In this case, it is appropriate to get training and expect reasonable regulation.
et's take a look at the reality of a dangerous sport like BASE jumping.
From 1997 to 2002, fatalities averaged nearly one fatality every two weeks.
The average BASE jumper has a nearly 50 percent likelihood of dying or being seriously injured over the course of a lifetime of jumping.
So why do people continue to jump?

Some jumpers say it is for the thrill, others because they value the freedom of parachuting on their own terms and don't want to be encumbered by gravity, and others simply want to experience flight without a plane.
I contend that these are good reasons and enough to support this activity as a sport.
In fact, one could argue that the seriousness of the risk makes it more fun and adventurous to many people.
If BASE jumping were as safe as golf, there wouldn't be the attraction for some to give it a try.
So is it selfish to participate in risky sports?
That depends on how you want to look at it.
I believe you need to make an informed choice and understand the risks.
Be smart about it, but don't be afraid to pursue your dreams and desires.

When you die, you appear in a cinema with a number of other people who look like you.
You find out that they are your previous reincarnations, and soon you all begin watching your next life on the big screen.
It can be somewhat unnerving to realize that this is how the end of your life will turn out.
Yet to be honest, this experience can also be a refreshing one.
In the movie, the characters are able to influence the events on the screen.
They can change the plot of their life, and even alter their own fate.

This means that in the movie, you might be able to resolve the issues that you had with the girl you got into a huge argument with and had a falling out with, or that guy you broke up with on bad terms, or that parent you had a bad relationship with that couldn't be fixed.
When you die, you will have the opportunity to resolve all of these issues.
You will be able to make amends with all of the people you have wronged, and you will be able to apologize to all of the people.
And in doing so, you will be able to forge a new path for yourself.
You will be able to come clean of your sins and you will be able to walk with much more confidence and pep as a result.
If you have a lot of unresolved issues in your life, it is a good idea to start resolving them now.
Of course the movie that will play at your life's end might be able to give you some sense of closure but it cannot necessarily be your fallback crutch.
After all, the people you have hurt or wronged in your current life deserve an apology from you now, while you are still living in the moment.
It is important to note that the movie that plays at your life's end is not necessarily a reflection of the life you have led.
Sometimes the movie's portrayal of you will not be accurate and this is to be expected.
After all, the movie is a reflection of your life as seen through the eyes of the people who were in your life.
This means that the movie could in some ways be a bit distorted.
You might feel betrayed in the way that some people view you and your life story, if others' perceptions don't align with your own.
However, even if the movie is not an accurate portrayal of your life, it is still a good idea to watch it.
This is because this exercise can be a hugely transformative experience.
It is also a humbling one, as it's so rare to get an objective third party view of yourself.
The movie that plays at your life's end is also a good opportunity to reflect on your life..
But the important thing to walk away with from this contemplation and reflection is that no one is perfect.
No one who watches the movie of their life will ever feel that the events in their life unfolded absolutely perfectly.
So if you are feeling a bit down about yourself and your life, it is important to remember that you are not alone.
Don't feel that you have let yourself down or let others down.
Also remember that any mistakes or flaws in the movie will be magnified.
So don't beat yourself up about it.
In conclusion, take this opportunity to view the movie of your life as one that is valuable to understand yourself and to understand the world around you.
This movie is a gift that you will be given when you die.
Make sure to use the time that you are given with this gift in a way that is meaningful.
This means that you should live your life in the present and make amends with people you hurt as soon as you can, before you reach the end of your life.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, it is arrogant and asinine to call any sport too dangerous to be considered a sport.
This is the same type of argument that can be used to deny someone the freedom to travel, because traveling can have criminal consequences.
The only thing that makes any sport dangerous, is when it is performed in a reckless manner.
One cannot simply call a sport, like mountain climbing, too dangerous to be considered a sport, without defining what is reckless about it.
If one calls mountain climbing too dangerous then they are literally saying that it is reckless to climb a mountain.
One cannot simply use the term reckless and make everyone agree on the same thing.
We all have different standards.
To assume that we all think the same is not only arrogant, but is also an injustice against us as a free country with the freedom to be different.
Calling a sport too dangerous to be considered a sport is asinine because the definition of sport has changed over the years.
People in the past considered sports to be things like bullfighting and gladiator fighting; things that many would consider reckless by today's standards.
Hunting, fishing, javelin-throwing and archery all involved substantial risk.
Ask a person from the early 1900's what sports are and they would probably say boxing, horseback riding, or hiking and skiing.
Teddy Roosevelt engaged in the 'sport' of big game hunting and one of his companions was killed by wildlife during one of his hunting 'safaris.'
When one calls a sport too dangerous to be considered a sport, they are effectively ruling out many of man's favorite pursuits throughout time.
Each person has their own definition of risk.
To each their own.
Just because someone thinks high-risk activities are reckless, does not necessarily mean everyone else feels the same way.
The most important thing in determining the value of a sport, is how the participants evaluate it on their own terms.
People evaluate something based on what they want out of life.
And we all have different values.

e will be able to go outside again, we will be able to travel again.

t's also nice not to have to sit still.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, to fully absorb a book you need to read it.
You can't get the full effect of a book by listening to it.

There are some positives to listening to a book, such as being able to listen to a book while doing other things, being able to listen in places where you could not read, such as being in the car, or being able to listen to a book when you are too tired to read.
However, all of these things point to the reason it is better to read a book.

To get the most from a book, it needs your fully attention, the things that make listening to it attractive also mean you are not fully engaged, you are doing other things that need some of your attention.
I believe if you listen to it, some of the content passes you by, you miss out on some of the finer details and you miss the nuances that make a book great.
Listening is useful, and a pleasant past time, but it is not the same as reading.
So while you can enjoy an audio book, you will not get the same experience as you would from reading the book.
That experience allows you to gain more from the written text and understand what the author is conveying.
So, in conclusion, I believe it is better to read a book than listen to it.

Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, the only form of compensation that an athlete should get is through a scholarship for tuition and lodging.
The NCAA should not pay athletes because it would ruin the integrity of the game.
After college, the players have the opportunity to sell their skills in professional sports.
The time for the athlete to capitalize on their sports skills should not be in college.
If college athletes are being paid, I think that puts the student in a very powerful position versus the school.
The student could demand more money, or even threaten to quit the team if they don't get what they want.
The contract disputes that we see today in professional sports would occur in college.
I think this would be detrimental for the colleges that are involved in situations like this.
Overall, I do find Cody McDavis' argument to be persuasive.
I do think that larger schools would have a huge advantage when attracting players.
If a school has access to large monetary resources, I think that increases the chances of the best athletes going to that school.
I think the smaller schools would be at a very large disadvantage.
Once the best athletes come to the bigger schools, there is a greater chance that school will be successful in athletic competitions.
This further increases the chance that the best athletes in the future will come to that school.
I think it would be very difficult to quantify how much to pay the students.
If you are not a well-known athlete, should you be paid the same as a more well-known athlete?
How do we quantify this?
I think it creates a lot of unnecessary headaches for the school.
Overall, I think it would be better to just give the athletes a scholarship.
There are far too many drawbacks and not enough positives to students being paid.
I think that colleges need to really think hard about this issue before moving forward.

Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, McDavis is right on point.
College athletes are still students, and should be treated as such; besides, providing money to student-athletes would only lead to further corruption.
No other students are actually paid for what they do in college, so why should these athletes be any different?
They already receive money to live on, and scholarships, what more could they want?

If they were paid to play sports, they'd not only be getting a free education, and the opportunity to do what they love, and the chance to make a lot of money someday as a professional, they'd be getting paid for the opportunity to do that, which is several bridges too far.

Also, I can't help that that would tend to breed resentment among the student-body; can you imagine being a student at a Division III school, having to work part-time jobs to pay for your classes, and seeing student athletes not only get free tuition, and breezing by in classes, but also getting paid for all that?
Given the political climates of today's campuses, it could easily lead to student revolts.
The real question here isn't whether student athletes should be paid.

The real question is  whether colleges should be in the business of running sports programs, serving as a training ground for pro sports, and relying upon the financial success of the students and the alumni to swell the coffers of the supposed 'educational institution.'

A follow up question to that, is should colleges that do that still be granted tax-exempt status or non-profit status, especially since such a large percentage of the earnings of those schools goes towards running the athletic programs?
Again, my answer to all these questions is a resounding, 'NO.'

However, if colleges are going to continue to operate in this way, they should at least maintain the pretense that they are in fact there to educate the students, not to provide a free source of labor and entertainment for them,  in order for them to still be considered schools at all.
It's marginal now; if they were to start paying students for playing sports, they're no longer schools.
They're just sports franchises, like any other, and they'd need to be licensed and regulated as such.

We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.

Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
Computers and phones are here to stay.

American adults need to worry less about our own screen time and more about letting children sit alone on screens all day.

t's all a matter of balance.

Screens can make you feel more isolated from your surrounding.

Screen time can be useful, to learn new things,  talk with family and friends, and enjoy innocent entertainment.
